articles.title: Airport X-ray exposes dangerous weapon illegally concealed in passenger's carry-on
articles.summary: TSA officers at New York's Watertown International Airport found a spent M18 smoke grenade inside a traveler's carry-on bag — and the person had a strange excuse.
articles.body: A routine security screening at upstate New York's Watertown International Airport (ART) took a startling turn when TSA officers discovered a spent smoke grenade hidden inside an aerosol container in a passenger's carry-on bag. The discovery was made by Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officers recently, according to a Sept. 24 release from the agency. During inspection, officers found the spent M18 smoke grenade. SHARP WEAPON DISCOVERED BY TSA TUCKED INSIDE UNUSUAL ITEM IN PASSENGER'S CARRY-ON BAG In a statement, TSA Officer Yessenia Alvarez, who was operating the X-ray machine at the time, said she "didn’t like how the item appeared," referring to the unusual-looking aerosol container. "I called over Lead TSA Officer Melissa Graffam and told her I did not have a good feeling about it," said Alvarez. "I was very stunned when I saw the item on the screen." The officer added that she had "seen these types of items in training scenarios." AIRPORT X-RAY REVEALS SHOCKING ILLEGAL STASH CONCEALED BESIDE PASSENGER'S XBOX Graffam said the item "looked funny" when she saw it on the X-ray screen. "I saw from the image that the top of the can didn’t look right but appeared to be empty," she said. "It was located in the side pocket of the bag, so I opened it and saw it was an M18 smoke grenade." Graffam said the discovery was particularly unusual for the small airport, where officers typically encounter prohibited items such as knives and oversized liquids. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER When she asked the passenger why the smoke grenade was in his bag, he told her he had forgotten it was there, according to the TSA. "I found [that] strange because his bag only had a few items in it," Graffam said. Lead TSA Officer Debra Alcock, who was serving as acting supervisor, then notified the Syracuse TSA Coordination Center and a TSA explosives expert — who confirmed the grenade was not live. The smoke grenade ranked among the most memorable finds Alcock has seen during her time with the agency, the release said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "The teamwork in resolving this issue was excellent," said Alcock. "Everyone did their part to help control the checkpoint while we resolved the situation." Brian Bushnell, TSA's federal security director for upstate New York's airports, said the incident serves as a reminder for travelers to check their bags before leaving home. "Spent, inert or replica explosive items are not allowed through the checkpoint and can cause delays, disrupt operations and prompt a law enforcement response," said Bushnell. "When in doubt, travelers should leave the item at home or check TSA’s resources, such as TSA.gov, before packing." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Though many people believe that spent grenades are not hazardous, officials warn that they can still pose risks. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) has issued public safety alerts regarding vintage grenades in particular. "Do not try to test the system." Recently, at Tampa International Airport, TSA officers discovered another alarming object. TSA Officer Andrew Carter was screening the passenger's carry-on bag with an X-ray machine when he noticed something unusual about the flashlight — and flagged the bag for a closer look. He ultimately found a 4-inch, double-edged knife concealed inside a baseball bat-shaped flashlight, according to an employee story published on the agency's website. "Do not try to test the system," Keith Jeffries, the Florida-based vice president of K2 Security Screening Group and a former federal security director for TSA at Los Angeles International Airport, told Fox News Digital about the knife incident. articles.title: Why electric cars might be making some passengers feel sick
articles.summary: “I’ve heard about it many, many, many times” says one doctor who treats motion sickness.
articles.body:
Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.

Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.

It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.

Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.

So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?

Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.

It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says.

"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.

But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.

Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point".

"There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.

'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell'

When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs.

Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.

She used to get motion sick only on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute drive to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.

On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.

Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars.

Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says.

But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue , telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds.

Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness.

Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles.

Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says.

Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the electric car starts to slow down and uses the energy to feed the battery. However, it is a process that needs to be done smoothly with the accelerator being released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration.

"It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac.

This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time".

Electric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness.

Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly.

She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself.

Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, Hac says. Women and children are more susceptible, experts say.

Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF.

Hold your head still and open the window

As their popularity increases, avoiding electric vehicles can be a challenge - the number of new zero-emission cars registered in the UK rose by 40.5% in April to June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, latest Department for Transport figures show.

At the end of June 2026, 5.8% of all licensed cars on UK roads were zero-emission vehicles, the data shows. The sale of new purely petrol or diesel cars is set to be banned from 2030.

Lucinda Harrison, 24, from London says she often books taxis that turn out to be electric vehicles, and has to endure the trip feeling nauseous, sweaty and clammy.

The thought of travelling in an EV fills her with dread, she says. Even just a five-minute lift from a colleague to a Tube station recently was enough to make her feel "horrific".

Academics say there are several steps passengers can take to reduce feelings of motion sickness.

Look out of the front window and don't look at your phone or read a book

Sit in the front passenger seat rather than in the back, if possible. If you do have to sit in the back, opt for the middle seat so you can still see out the front window

Keep your head still by holding it against the headrest

Take travel sickness tablets if needed, though these can cause drowsiness

Before a long journey, make sure you're hydrated, have slept well and have eaten non-greasy food

Experts also say we can become desensitised to motion sickness through prolonged exposure. The more journeys you take in electric vehicles, the less likely you are to become motion sick as your body adjusts, Golding says.

There are also things carmakers can do to alleviate motion sickness in electric vehicles, says Prof Cyriel Diels, professor of mobility design at the Royal College of Art. These include having software that smooths out rapid acceleration, adding sound systems and subtle seat vibrations to signal to passengers that the car is moving, and offering adaptive regenerative braking that reduces sudden deceleration.

Matt Adams from BEAMA, which represents UK manufacturers of electric vehicle charge points, says he's confident that "if future research identifies the reason for car sickness that vehicle manufacturers can respond and improve accordingly".

But for Lola, she just wants her boyfriend to trade in his car. She says that day can't come soon enough.

articles.title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills
articles.summary: Immediate action is needed to help households struggling with bills this winter, says trade body Energy UK.
articles.body:
The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said.

Energy UK said domestic gas prices, which rose on Thursday, and forecasts of steep rises in January meant inaction would lead to a longer-term, more costly and deeper crisis.

Figures revealed by the BBC earlier this week showed forecasters predicting a 16% rise in domestic energy prices in the new year for 20 million households on variable tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was considering any measure that took the pressure off.

Households in England, Scotland and Wales on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity, were hit with a 4% price increase at the start of October.

That is the equivalent of about £60 per year - or £5 per month - taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Consultancy Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggested the same typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.

Energy UK said it accepted the government had already provided some support. VAT on electricity bills was cut on Thursday, and some levies were cancelled or shifted into taxation earlier this year.

But the trade body said these savings had been wiped out by high wholesale prices, paid by suppliers, that were the result in part of international events - namely conflict in the Middle East and the disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

It said bills were soaring as they had in 2022 when they were driven up by the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

"We cannot afford to wait for the same scale of crisis before acting again. We must heed the lessons from that time," said Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK.

She said that the urgent intervention needed was highlighted by growing levels of customer debt, the cost of which now added an average of £67 a year to everyone's bills.

Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years

Energy bills are rising by £60 a year - here's how you can bring that down

On Thursday, the boss of supplier EDF Energy, Simone Rossi, warned that the UK was "walking into a second energy crisis" and Vyas said that action was needed before bills jumped again.

"Last-minute emergency interventions run the risk of being badly targeted and costing us all more," she said.

Energy UK is calling for government measures including:

targeted support over and above the £150 Warm Home Discount, given to people on benefits, which would eventually lead to the introduction of a discounted social tariff

a debt relief scheme for the most severely affected households as part of a strategy that will also help prevent debt build-up among new tenants and homeowners

removing more levies from electricity bills and shifting them to taxation, as part of a wider move to electrification

At the Labour Party conference last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that he would not call Rossi's crisis warning an overstatement, adding that the cost of home energy, as well as petrol and diesel, was "very difficult indeed".

"We're looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off," he said.

articles.title: Two Iranians charged over alleged plot targeting Jewish community in UK
articles.summary: Two Iranian men are accused of preparing to commit an act of terrorism in Manchester ahead of Yom Kippur.
articles.body:
British authorities have charged two Iranian nationals with planning a terrorist attack against the Jewish community in northern England.

The UK Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said on Friday that Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with preparing to commit or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism in Manchester “on or before” Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, which began at sundown on September 20.

“It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot,” police said in a separate statement on Friday.

Details of the alleged plot have not been released, but police have confirmed its “disruption”.

Counterterrorism police said Salehi and Ahmadyan, both arrested in Manchester on September 20, allegedly tried to acquire components and equipment to make an improvised explosive device and conducted reconnaissance on potential targets for attack.

The pair will appear at London’s Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Saturday, the CPS said.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said Salehi and Ahmadyan arrived in the UK on a small boat from Europe several years ago. One of the men had been granted asylum and the other had a live asylum claim, the Home Office said.

“It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime,” she said in a statement.

“They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement,” she added.

The charges come a year after two people were killed in a knife and gun attack by a British citizen of Syrian descent at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in northern Manchester on October 2, 2025.

“I’m aware that the news of this alleged plot coming during the High Holy day period has caused a great deal of concern to the Jewish community, as well as with the wider public,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said on Friday.

“It also coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing antisemitic incidents across the UK.”

Detectives said there was no connection between Friday’s charges and the suspected plot involving the RAF Fairford air base, over which a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on Thursday, according to the Reuters news agency.

Britain said Tehran had been involved in an alleged plot earlier this week targeting an air base used by the US to launch attacks against Iran.

Iran denied any involvement in the RAF Fairford plot and said speculation would “fuel Iranophobia propaganda”.

articles.title: Deadly bear attacks are rattling Russian Siberia. Why now?
articles.summary: When Sofa, 28, was sent a video of a bear in the yard of her former home in central Siberia, it made her sit up. The threat they posed had once seemed distant.
articles.body: When Sofa, 28, was sent a video of a bear in the yard of her former home in central Siberia, it made her sit up. The threat they posed had once seemed distant. “We were never afraid to go outside, even at night,” she told CNN. A bear entering the yard was something she “couldn’t even imagine.” The unexpected sighting comes at a time when bear attacks are on the rise, with at least 16 fatal encounters across Russia in September, according to a CNN tally of Russian media reports. The country typically records 20 to 30 attacks on people annually, its Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment told state news agency TASS. This year, bears ventured into populated areas in more than 40 Russian regions, TASS reported. But it is central Siberia’s huge Krasnoyarsk region that has seen the highest death toll, with seven people killed. Last week, a bear fatally mauled a 51-year-old woman as she stepped out of her house there. Two days earlier, a security guard was killed in a bear attack at a truck parking lot in a forestry area. Earlier in September, two elderly women who had separately gone missing while out picking mushrooms were found dead, with injuries consistent with a bear attack. Fatal encounters were also reported in other Siberian regions. In neighboring Tuva, the father of Russian NHL player Andrei Kuzmenko was killed at the end of September after being attacked by a bear during a fishing trip. He was taken to a hospital with serious facial injuries but died shortly afterward, according to TASS. And in August, in the popular tourist spot of Altai, in southern Siberia, a bear tore open a tent and dragged a 29-year-old woman into the forest and killed her. Why are bears coming closer to people? Sergey Kolchin, a zoologist at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Far Eastern Branch who specializes in large carnivores, said attacks on average had not become more frequent, but there had been a shift in certain Siberian regions this year, particularly Krasnoyarsk. Konstantin Tirronen, head of zoology at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Karelian Research Center, offered a slightly different assessment, saying attacks this year were above the annual average, though concentrated in specific regions. Both linked the situation to an unusually poor autumn crop of pine nuts and berries. Kolchin also cited extensive wildfires that had deprived some bears of their habitat as a compounding effect. “Trying to make up for food shortages, bears are increasingly venturing into areas used by people, where encounters are inevitable,” he told CNN. Tirronen added that bears intensify their search for food as they build up fat reserves for winter hibernation. “If there is little food in the wild, they will look for it anywhere they can,” he explained. He also suggested that accessible food waste and the expansion of extractive industries into previously remote wildlife habitats were factors bringing bears and people into closer contact. “We are creating attractive food sources that draw them in,” Tirronen said. “The responsibility here lies with people, not with bears.” Dmitry Sergeev, a natural resources official in Khakassia, in southern Siberia, called the rise “abnormal.” “The bear population is above normal levels. Stronger animals are displacing weaker ones. There is not enough room for them, so they are moving closer to people,” he told Russian pro-Kremlin broadcaster REN TV. But both experts CNN spoke with cautioned against linking increased attacks to a growing bear population, citing a lack of reliable population estimates. Bears’ solitary nature and winter hibernation make them difficult to count, Tirronen explained. Can culling solve the problem? Over the past two months, authorities in at least 10 regions across Siberia and the Russian Far East have issued warnings to residents over increased bear activity. Nighttime curfews were also imposed in parts of Altai and in Baikalsk, in the Irkutsk region. Meanwhile, officials in Krasnoyarsk have closed the Krasnoyarsk Pillars National Park and the Torgashinsky Ridge Staircase, a popular hiking route. Regional authorities have also deployed mobile hunting teams and offered cash rewards for killing bears. In the Krasnoyarsk region, where most of the fatal attacks have occurred, rewards of more than 35,000 roubles (around $420) were announced. Altai’s natural resources ministry said more than 50 bears were killed following the tourist’s death in August, with permits issued to cull another 157. Krasnoyarsk’s natural resources ministry said earlier this month that more than 180 “potentially problematic animals” had been killed. Killing aggressive bears in populated areas is a necessary emergency measure, Kolchin said. But a more widespread cull would not reduce incidents in the long term, he argued, because it fails to address their root cause: unsecured food waste. “Other bears will take the place of those killed near rubbish dumps,” he said. “Widespread, indiscriminate shooting of bears amid the current hysteria will leave wounded animals that can be deadly.” According to Kolchin, wounded bears struggle to survive in the wild and are more likely to attack people in self-defense. Animals that associate their injuries with humans, he said, can also become more aggressive toward people. Instead, he said, the solution lies in keeping waste out of reach, teaching people how to behave around wildlife and using deterrents such as electric fencing to avoid encounters in the future.

images.caption: A brown bear strolls through Norilsk in Krasnoyarsk region in May 2022. The region, home to one of Russia's largest brown bear populations, saw seven fatal bear attacks in September alone.
Krasnoyarsk Pillars National Park, on the outskirts of the Siberian city of Krasnoyarsk, is closed to visitors until October 25 due to bear sightings.

articles.title: Woman deceived ex-partner that she gave birth to his babies, judge rules
articles.summary: The man paid his ex-partner around £30,000 over two years believing she had given birth to his children.
articles.body:
A woman convinced her former partner she had given birth to two children who most likely did not exist in what a High Court judge described as an "extraordinary" and "elaborate campaign of deceit".

The man, who has not been named but was referred to as John during the hearing, applied to the Family Court after he was told the woman had sold their two children for a combined £500.

The case heard that the man received messages and photos of the children and paid the woman around £30,000 over the course of two years.

But in a hearing in February, the woman, who was referred to as Jane, told the judge she had lied about the pregnancies for revenge, claiming the man had abused her.

The court heard the man believed he was the children's' father because in late 2022 his partner told him she was pregnant, sent pictures of an ultrasound image and had become "visibly pregnant" as time went on.

In May 2023, shortly before the first baby was due, the woman called the police alleging she had been assaulted by the man.

He was arrested and subsequently held on remand for several months, Mrs Justice Judd said in her ruling which was published on Friday.

Following this, the woman sent a message to his stepfather saying the baby had been born as well as sharing baby photos.

At one stage she is said to have sent voice notes to her former partner's mother in the middle of the night with the sound of a baby crying in the background.

Later, she told the man she was pregnant again and the baby was due in August 2024.

However, before the due date, the couple split up and did not reconcile.

The woman would go on to tell the man's mother the baby had been born.

The woman admitted to the court she had told him she was pregnant when they were together, and afterwards, but conceded she had told a series of elaborate lies and that there were, in fact, no children.

She argued she was menopausal at the time and could not have been pregnant and bank statements show she attended a tanning shop on the day she said she had given birth, Mrs Justice Judd said.

In her judgement, the judge concluded that the "factors that weigh against the children genuinely existing were very strong, stronger than the factors pointing the other way".

She said the man was the victim of a "sustained and elaborate campaign of deceit" which also impacted his mother and closest friend.

"Added to this, the behaviour was cruel, leading a man and his mother to believe they had children and grandchildren respectively.", the Judge said.

The judge added she was unable to conclude the woman's motive for her behaviour but said financial fraud was a "possibility" and that the "complex mental health problems" she suffered from may have also played a part.

articles.title: WHO warns of ‘devastating consequences’ due to delayed aid entry into Gaza
articles.summary: The WHO’s representative in Palestine calls on Israeli authorities to ‘release the pressure on medical supplies’.
articles.body:
Repeated delays in bringing life-saving medicines, prosthetics and other supplies from Israel into Gaza risk having “devastating consequences” for Palestinians who urgently need them, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.

Approved aid can enter Gaza only through Kerem Shalom, at the southern tip of the territory, while Rafah, also in the south, is open only for limited movement of people, including patients needing medical treatment abroad, the WHO said on Friday.

“A truck full of non-priority supplies or the right supplies arriving too late , doesn’t save lives. That’s the question that actually matters,” Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, the WHO’s representative in Palestine, said.

Van De Weerdt called on Israeli authorities to “release the pressure on medical supplies”, saying essential medicines “should not be considered as dual use, as they are globally accepted standards on medical items anybody needs anywhere to run a hospital or a clinic”.

She added that one shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices had been rejected four times over the past six months.

“Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again,” she said, noting that medicines “by contrast, move relatively well”, with almost 87 percent approved and just over 1 percent rejected.

“Our ask is simple and has not changed: we need the unimpeded and predictable entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza at scale. We also need a multi-crossing model so that aid isn’t forced to trickle down through a limited number of crossings,” Van De Weerdt said.

Four other main entry points into Gaza – Kissufim, Gate 96, Erez and Erez West – remain closed and under total Israeli control.

She praised the “extraordinary health workers” still risking their lives in Gaza, who she said were not receiving enough supplies to give patients the care they needed.

“As winter begins, this urgency to get supplies into Gaza only deepens,” Van De Weerdt said. “Almost two million people are in need of shelter to protect against the cold and the risk of flooding, exposing people to serious health and safety risks, let alone their dignity.”

She said residents faced a heightened risk of preventable disease outbreaks linked to the lack of safe shelter and clean water, and a high number of rats whose bites transmit infection, a threat made harder to track by the destruction of public health laboratories.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned on Thursday of serious public health risks from the accumulation of solid waste in Gaza City, where sanitation gains remain fragile because of a lack of reliable access to heavy machinery, engine oil, spare parts and fuel funding.

Almost 12 months into a fragile “ceasefire” between Hamas and Israel, marked by continuing Israeli air attacks and other military activity, Gaza’s humanitarian situation remains “overwhelming”, according to OCHA.

articles.title: The vetting gap: How an Omani flagged for extremism ended up piloting a Tel Aviv-bound flydubai jet
articles.summary: Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of stabbing Captain Smit Machchhar and attempting to crash a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, had already
articles.body: Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of stabbing Captain Smit Machchhar and attempting to crash a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, had already come to the attention of authorities for his radical extremist tendencies. Despite this he was cleared to fly to Israel by flydubai.Investigators are trying to establish how an Omani pilot ended up as first officer on a flight to Israel, given that Israel and Oman do not have diplomatic relations.Hamam al-Hammami's backgroundAl-Hammami is a 29-year-old Omani national, according to US media reports. He entered pilot training with Oman Air and worked for the airline for several years. A LinkedIn profile bearing his name, which CNN said was verified by a source as belonging to him, showed a seven-year stint at Oman Air ending in February 2025. It also listed a subsequent job with Royal Air Maroc, from June 2025 to January 2026. The profile has since been deleted.Investigators are also examining social-media material attributed to al-Hammami.A deleted video showed Israeli aircraft in Dubai and ended with images of former al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri and al-Qaeda-linked suicide bomber Humam Khalil Abu-Mulal al-Balawi.Another post featured an AI-generated image of Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem accompanied by a poem about rejecting humiliation and not fearing death. CNN said it remained unclear who posted the material or whether the posts had been scheduled as they were posted after the flydubai incident.CNN also analysed thousands of deleted posts attributed to al-Hammami, including material expressing strongly misogynistic and conservative views.How did he get into the cockpit?The question about his presence on a flight headed towards Tel Aviv arose because Oman does not have diplomatic relations with Israel, yet al-Hammami was serving as a co-pilot on a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight operated by a UAE airline.Israeli authorities are investigating how he came to be assigned to the flight and whether aviation-security procedures were followed.CBS News reported that sources initially suggested al-Hammami could have held dual citizenship, which they said might explain how he was cleared to fly to Israel.He was born in the UAE to an Omani father and Syrian mother and spent much of his life outside Oman, according to sources cited by CNN.However, a later report by Jerusalem Post citing people familiar with the investigation said he did not have a second nationality, leaving the question of how he was cleared unresolved.According to sources cited by CBS News, Omani government surveillance found that al-Hammami was visiting radical websites while he was undergoing pilot training.Oman Air subsequently transferred him from flying duties to an administrative role.One source said he later resigned from the airline after being placed on desk duty and left around 2024.Other reports have described him as having been barred or suspended from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views.After leaving Oman Air, al-Hammami moved to Dubai and eventually joined flydubai.Sources told CBS News that flydubai hired him without vetting him through the Omani government.That has become one of the central questions in the investigation: whether information about his earlier removal from flying duties was passed on to his subsequent employers or relevant security authorities.It remains unclear what background checks were conducted when he joined flydubai.What are investigators probing now?Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said investigators believe al-Hammami underwent Islamist radicalisation and was trying to crash the aircraft with its passengers. He has also said authorities are examining whether he was sent by someone else.US president Donald Trump separately suggested that al-Hammami could be linked to Iran, although Netanyahu has said it was too early to determine whether Iran was involved.The UAE has opened an investigation into whether the attack involved terrorist activity, prior planning or outside direction, while Israeli authorities are examining how al-Hammami came to be part of the flight crew.You use AI every day. articles.title: Brazil XI vs India – Predicted lineup and team news
articles.summary: On Saturday, India and Brazil will meet for the first time ever in a senior men’s international friendly at Kolkata’s Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan (Sal...
articles.body:
On Saturday, India and Brazil will meet for the first time ever in a senior men's international friendly at Kolkata's Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan (Salt Lake Stadium).

Brazil arrive in strong condition, having gone through their last six games with the record L-W-W-W-D-W. After a disappointing round-of-16 elimination by Norway at the 2026 World Cup, the Seleção have regrouped under head coach Carlo Ancelotti. In their most recent international window, they played two friendlies against Australia: the opening match ended in a close 1–1 draw, while the return fixture saw Brazil run out comfortable 4–2 winners.

Ancelotti will be missing Barcelona winger Raphinha, who pulled out of the 26-player experimental squad because of a right-thigh injury sustained against Australia; he has returned to Spain for treatment, and no replacement has been summoned.

Raphinha joins Chelsea's Joao Pedro and Roma's Wesley on the injury list for this camp. Even without them, Brazil's roster remains packed with elite talent, led by Real Madrid star Vinicius Junior and teenage forwards Endrick and Estevao Willian.

At the back, seasoned defenders Marquinhos and Gabriel Magalhaes are expected to lead the line, while Arsenal midfielder Bruno Guimaraes is set to dictate play in the centre of the park.

Fluminense forward Gabriel Martinelli has been added to the squad as a late call-up. Ancelotti is likely to deploy an attacking 4-3-3 formation aimed at controlling possession and making the most of wide areas.

As overwhelming favourites, Brazil are expected to use their technical quality and intense pressing to try to unsettle India's defence from the outset

Possible Brazil starting XI: Souza; Matheuzinho, Marquinhos, Gabriel, D Santos; A Santos, Martinelli, Guimares; Estevao, Vinicius, Endrick

The match will kick off at 3pm BST on Saturday, 3rd October.

There is no official television channel or mainstream broadcaster showing the India vs Brazil friendly live in the United Kingdom. In India, the host broadcaster for the match is the Sony Sports Network, with coverage across its Sony Sports channels and streaming on SonyLIV.
